chunks: "With a single low-side switch I can only coast: turn it off and the motor spins down on friction, which can take seconds.
To brake I need a path that lets the motor's own back-EMF drive current through something that dissipates the energy. The simplest way is to short the motor terminals.
A spinning motor is a generator, so shorting it makes a current of E over R flow, which creates a torque opposing rotation.
In a half-bridge with the motor to ground, I turn on the low-side FET and switch off the high side. In an H-bridge I turn on both low-side FETs, or both high-side FETs.
For a 12 volts motor with 0. 02 volts per rad per second and 1 ohm winding at 3,000 rpm, E is 6. 3 volts so the brake current starts at 6.
3 amps and decays exponentially with a time constant of about 50 milliseconds for a small rotor, versus a full second coasting.
Things I'd watch: the brake current can be larger than the running current, so the FETs and winding need to take it, or I PWM the brake to limit it.
Braking torque falls to zero with speed, so it can't hold a load at standstill; I'd need a mechanical brake or an active hold.
If I want a faster stop, I can briefly reverse the voltage, plugging, but then I must cut the drive at zero speed or it spins up backwards.
And with regenerative braking the energy goes back into the supply, so if the supply can't absorb it the bus voltage can rise dangerously."
